title: PETER HOSKIN reviews Sid Meier's Civilization VII: Civilization marches on - but sometimes, as in the case of Civ VII, 'progress' makes you pine for the past…
text:
By Peter Hushin
Published: 00:13 GMT, February 14, 2025 | Updated: 00:14 GMT, February 14, 2025
Sid Meier’s Civilization VII (PlayStation, Xbox, Switch, PC, £ 59.99)
VERDICT: Less civilized
Classification:
The launch of a new title in the 34 -year -old civilization series is always quite something. It is an event. A monument in the landscape of the games.
But it is also a kind of decrease.
After years of playing the previous civilization and seeing it grow with multiple expansions and additional nations and additional game modes, throughout a sequel that takes away much of that and begins from scratch. Again.
That feeling, of something lost and cattle, is particularly acute in the case of civilization VII. More than any other civil launch before, he made me want to have stayed with the previous incarnation.

Not that Civ VII is terrible. His basic game, progress of a civilization through history at the expense of other weakest civilizations, remains convincing.
And their updated graphics are beautiful.
There are even some winning innovations, including the way in which history is now divided into three different ages, which forces it to adopt a new culture to the passage of each. This shakes a game that could otherwise have been tired.
No, it is more than Civ VII has been simplified to the point of … on -complexity.
Information about cities and buildings and people who used to be a single click of the mouse has now hidden in Submenus within Submenus. It looks cleaner, but plays a lot, much more messy.
The result is that civil games such as the humanity of 2021 and ARA: the history of last year’s history now seem less suitors to the throne, and more as monarchs waiting.
If civilization, or history, in fact, has taught us anything, is that dynasties fall.
